questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Interesting courses offered, English language, and a country with a nature and activities I can explore

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, during the international orientation week we received a folder and had a lot of information lectures with the necessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I arrived a few weeks before the semester started and I didn't receive any assistance then. However, we received a lot of information during the international orientation week. I rented a room in a flat privately, so it might be different if you stay at a hall of residence.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I became a member of different facebook groups, e.g. Vic deals, Flats and Rooms for Rent Wellington NZ, etc., and contacted people posting about a room there. I was in touch with different people for a few weeks, when I was still in Denmark and had virtual viewings. I finally found a place with great flatmates a month before arriving in Wellington. It's also possible to arrive a few weeks before and stay at a hostel while you look at rooms in the city. However, it was very easy to find one once you invested some time in it.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I stayed in a flat with kiwis and I feel like I got a more authentic look into how it is to live like a local in Wellington. I also got on well with my flatmates who invited me to stuff with their friends. However, if you don't find a flat like that and you'd like to find friends, it's much easier in halls of residence with other exchange students. At times, I did feel like I was missing out on what the other exchange students got up to - but I think it had more to do with me being very busy with uni work compared to the other exchange students who were mostly undergraduates. We had different social whatsapp groups where exchange students (at least in the beginning) shared some activities you could join. The actual university did not arrange many social gatherings (if any). All in all, I really enjoyed living off campus in a private flat: I was social with local kiwis, it was cheaper, and I became more acquainted with the kiwi way of life.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not spend much time in the halls of residence so I wouldn't know how it was actually like living there. But I chose flatting privately for the reasons mentioned above and because the students living in the halls tended to be around 5 years younger. However, I know that a lot of the exchange students liked living there, especially the social aspects of it.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was quite difficult to find courses that could be pre-approved by the University of Copenhagen - but this wasn't Vic Uni's fault, I just had to go back and forth between the different universities a few times.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I had to register for courses through an online form on VUW's student portal. I was able to do that after I received pre-approval for courses by UCPH. You had to fill in different courses you wanted and they would decide which ones you were eligible for and enrol you in them. I was enrolled in a few wrong ones because you couldn't specify which you would like to replace others. After applying for changes to the enrolment, I received an email from the Student Success Advisor who helped me finalise the process by enrolling me in courses that still had spots left.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You had to do the research on which courses you'd be able to take, based on pre-requisites at the host university and whether the courses could be approved as the compulsory courses you would have needed to take at your home university in that semester.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: It was a long process but I ended up with the courses I wanted and needed.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Make sure you have as many courses as possible pre-approved by your home university, it makes the process a lot easier.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The learning style was different than back home and I had to get used to that at first. I feel like we didn't learn theories that deeply but more how to reflect on them.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Most of the courses I took consisted of the students discussing their own opinions on the course readings, rather than learning theories and the application of them. 3 out of 4 of the courses was mostly comprised of 40-minute presentations on course readings by student peers followed by class discussions. It would have been nice if the lecturers taught the class more. We also had many small assignments, I think I had 2-3 assignments each week, which took up a lot my time.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: At Vic Uni, there was a lot of focus on the students expressing their opinions on theories, rather than diving into their meaning and how to use them practically. At UCPH, we focus a lot more on the latter.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PSYC405: Environmental Psychology
PSYC411: Behavioural Analysis: Translating from Experiment to Analysis
PSYC423: Culture and Social Behaviour
PSYC431: Culture and Human Development

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I think all of the courses were worth it, e.g. learning about cultures when you're experiencing a new culture was very fitting. However, my favourite course was PSYC411: Behavioural Analysis: Translating from Experiment to Analysis, as the class had the Department of Conservation (DOC) as a partner and had to help solve a human behaviour problem they faced. In the beginning we were presented with different behaviour theories but we were free to identify theories and models that could help solve the problem. It was a very collaboratively based class as we were divided into groups, and felt a lot like an actual work project you could have as a psychologist working with behaviour change projects.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I bought a used car and had to pay an insurance excess when I reversed into a fence one time, haha. But other than that, I didn't really have any unexpected costs. But if you buy a used car, make sure you buy excess-free insurance, 5 dollars extra every second week is worth not having to pay unexpected excesses. Also, it was very easy to resell the car when you have to leave - I sold it on Facebook Marketplace.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Vegetables are expensive! However, there is a market on the waterfront every Sunday where vegetables are slightly cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a recreational centre with a lot of different clubs and sports you can try. I didn't sign up for it since the gym was a bit too small for me. I became a member of CityFitness instead, which is a big gym chain in New Zealand.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I also signed up for Wellington Boxing Gym in town. It has such a cool vibe, and you can either get a 10 training pass or sign up for 3 months. Every Monday you could also go there for free. One of the best things I did! I hadn't tried boxing before but the Boxfit class was more a combination between boxing and fitness and it was a lot of fun and the 45-minutes went by very fast.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
To be honest, there is so much to see around New Zealand. Here is a few highlights:

Around Wellington:
- Go to Mt Vic lookout
- Visit some of the local breweries!
- Concerts at the San Fran venue on Cuba St
- Walk the Skyline track (or at least some of it)

Around NZ:
- Definitely Queenstown on the South Island, it's a town full of different adventure activities, fx bungy jump, white water rafting, canyoning, mountain biking, wine tours
- If you can go on a road trip by either renting or buying a camper van, do that!
- Skiing during the NZ winter! Either Mt Ruapehu (North Island) or around Queenstown (South Island)
- Rotorua: Geysers!
- Hobbiton
- Waitomo glowworm caves- I tried blackwater rafting here!
- West Coast (driving along the coast!)
- Fiordland: either Milford Sound or if you have time: Doubtful Sound (accessible by ferry)
- Mt Cook (try the Hooker Valley Track on a good day for incredible views of mountains, glaciers, a lake and a river! Unreal!)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Rent a room privately! The exchange students staying in the halls mostly socialised with other exchange students. But if you want to get to know locals, a great way is to live with them. You can talk to some of them in class, but it will be hard to socialise with them outside of classes.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Not really anything - the culture is quite similar to the Danish culture.
Also remember to indicate to the bus that you want to get on by holding out your arm and remember to say thank you to the driver when leaving the bus.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: That they are more open to different cultures due to their bicultural heritage.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Remember to see more of the country than just Wellington!
Have access to a car!
Be ready for the weather to change from sunny to basically a storm in 5 minutes!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do some research about what you want to see and do in New Zealand. The months fly by so fast!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know my flatmates and experiencing what New Zealand has to offer

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The time difference to back home. You feel very distant from Denmark when people are mostly sleeping when you are awake. But it's fine when you're keeping busy!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
